clue.text: Artillery inspection by planning authority

definitions.note: taken loosely: the body that maps Britain, whose maps planners rely on

parts.note: ordnance is military artillery and munitions
a survey is an inspection or examination

explanation.surface: Big guns are being examined by the local council's planning department.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ordnance Survey is Britain's national mapping agency; the clue stretches that to a 'planning authority' since maps are what planning starts from.
explanation.definitionFit: The national mapping agency produces the maps on which British land planning is based, hence a loose planning body.

clue.text: Propose politician to fight for charity

definitions.note: a container meaning one for charitable gifts

parts.note: to propose is to offer
a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party
to box is to fight with fists

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a Conservative MP should enter the ring to raise money for good causes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the box's purpose: a church collection box, used for charity.
explanation.definitionFit: A church collection box receives worshippers' donations, money given as charitable offerings.

clue.text: Grain of the French spirit

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'
rum is a distilled spirit

explanation.surface: A question about which cereal the French favour, or what their essence is.
explanation.definitionFit: Durum is a hard wheat variety used for pasta, a cereal crop.

clue.text: Toothless creature from Texas town including old copper with right to move

indicators.note: the letter for right is told to shift its position within the town's name
the town's name takes in the coin's letter

parts.note: Amarillo is a city in Texas
d was the abbreviation for a penny, an old copper coin in pre-decimal British money

explanation.surface: A description of some Texan creature linked to a town, an old policeman and a right of movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old copper' suggests a retired policeman but is D, the old penny. AMARILLO with D inside gives AMADRILLO; 'to move' shifts its R up to second place.
explanation.definitionFit: Armadillos belong to the edentates, a group whose name literally means without teeth, though few lack them entirely.

clue.text: Garland parking in Swiss Cottage

indicators.note: the parking letter is placed inside the cottage word

parts.note: a chalet is a Swiss mountain cottage
P is the map and road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: Flowers hung where cars park at Swiss Cottage, an area of north London.
explanation.walkthrough: Swiss Cottage is a district of London, which makes it read like a place name rather than a definition of a chalet.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a wreath or circlet of flowers worn on the head.

clue.text: Nut, alas not exactly fruit

indicators.note: the letters are not given exactly as written, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sadly, a nut is not quite the same as a fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: NUT plus ALAS rearranged by 'not exactly' gives the dried grape.
explanation.definitionFit: A sultana is a dried seedless grape, a dried fruit used in baking.

clue.text: Come again about a dog

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A dog returns, or someone asks for a repeat about one.
explanation.definitionFit: To recur is to happen again or return repeatedly.

clue.text: Free tax cert? That is wrong

indicators.note: the letters are put in the wrong order and must be rearranged

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether a tax certificate is wrong and should be cancelled.
explanation.definitionFit: To extricate is to release or disentangle, to set free from difficulty.

clue.text: Meeting with I can't think what purpose

parts.note: 'what for?' asks the purpose, so for stands for purpose here
um is the sound of someone hesitating while thinking

explanation.surface: Someone at a meeting cannot work out its point.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a gathering or assembly for public discussion.

clue.text: Place everything and nothing with Blanchett

parts.note: all means everything
O looks like zero, nothing
Cate Blanchett is an Australian actress

explanation.surface: Finding a seat for the whole lot, a zero and a film star.
explanation.definitionFit: To allocate is to assign or place something in a set position.

clue.text: Dine out with writer to study Church's self-government

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the eating word are disordered

parts.note: a pen is a writing implement
a den is a study, a private room for work
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Going out to eat with an author to discuss the Church's freedom from state control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges DINE as INDE; 'study' is the room, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Independence is the condition of governing oneself without outside control.

clue.text: What Cameron & Co want to do with society is mere old cobblers

definitions.text: What Cameron & Co want to do with society

indicators.note: British slang for nonsense, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A political jibe that the Conservative leadership's plans for society are mere old nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cobblers' is British slang for rubbish, signalling the anagram of MERE OLD. David Cameron led the Conservatives with talk of reshaping 'Big Society'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cameron's party spoke of reshaping British society, which is to reshape or rebuild it.

clue.text: Call to account for a weather report

indicators.note: a report is a noise, so the phrase is heard rather than seen

parts.note: rain is one kind of weather, giving a rain

explanation.surface: Blaming the forecaster for the weather bulletin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like the weather report but signals what is heard: 'a rain' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To arraign is to bring someone before a court to answer charges.

clue.text: College could be holier without its head

indicators.note: the remaining letters could be rearranged into another word
the word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a college might be more saintly if it lost its principal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without its head' drops H from HOLIER, leaving OLIER, which 'could be' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriel is one of the colleges of Oxford University.

clue.text: Telling to modify bankers' bonuses?

definitions.note: taken as an adjective describing such bonuses

indicators.note: to modify the letters is to change their order

explanation.surface: Telling bankers to change their bonus payouts.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the definition is an example: the setter's view that bankers' bonuses are obtained dishonestly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-gotten describes gains acquired by dubious means, a jibe at lavish banking payouts.

clue.text: Exclusive brand meant dear product

indicators.note: a product is something made, here made from the letters

explanation.surface: An exclusive label meant an expensive item.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade name is a proprietary brand name owned exclusively by its maker.

clue.text: Impression of burial?

parts.note: an impression is a printed picture, and the word split as ... playfully suggests putting into a grave

explanation.definitionFit: An engraving is a print made from an incised plate, an impression.

clue.text: Hue and cry, having nothing to desire

parts.note: to yell is to cry out
O looks like zero, nothing
a wish is a desire

explanation.surface: An outcry with nothing to want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hue and cry' is a stock phrase, but here 'Hue' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellowish describes a colour tending to yellow, a shade or tint.

clue.text: Favour old dean holding up London gate

indicators.note: the dean's name holds the gate's letters within it

parts.note: William Inge, the 'gloomy dean', was Dean of St Paul's early in the twentieth century

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read bottom to top

parts.note: Ludgate was one of the gates of the City of London

explanation.surface: An old cathedral dean is favoured while holding up traffic at a London gate.
explanation.walkthrough: Dean Inge of St Paul's is a crossword favourite. 'Up' turns LUD into DUL, which INGE holds.
explanation.definitionFit: To indulge someone is to favour or gratify them.

clue.text: Composer includes first sonata as inaugural gift

indicators.note: the composer's name takes the letter inside

parts.note: George Frideric Handel was a Baroque composer

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the musical piece is used

explanation.surface: A composer includes his first sonata as a gift at an opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A handsel is a gift marking a new beginning, such as a new year or venture.

clue.text: Diver recoiled from iceberg

indicators.note: to recoil is to spring back, so the letters run backwards
the letters come out of the iceberg word

explanation.surface: Something that dives drew back sharply from an iceberg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diver' suggests a person, but it is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Grebes are diving water birds.

clue.text: Pompous like a barrel that's stuck in revolving door?

indicators.note: the barrel word is lodged inside the turned door
revolving turns the letters around into a new order

parts.note: a tun is a large barrel or cask

explanation.surface: Someone fat as a barrel gets jammed in a revolving door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like a barrel' hints at ROTUND, a false trail. 'Revolving' rearranges DOOR to OROD, with TUN 'stuck in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Orotund describes a style of speech that is pompous and bombastic.

clue.text: Empty post of international official?

definitions.note: a verb phrase meaning to strip a post of its men

parts.note: UN is the United Nations, an international body
man in the sense of an agent or official, as in 'our man in Geneva'

explanation.surface: A post held by an international official lies vacant.
explanation.walkthrough: Unman, in its older sense, is to remove the men from a fort or ship, leaving the post empty.
explanation.definitionFit: To unman a position is to deprive it of its personnel, leaving it unstaffed.

clue.text: Can nude dancing be subtly different?

indicators.note: dancing letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: Asking whether naked dancing can be done with finesse.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuanced means marked by fine shades of difference.

clue.text: Rise of Conservative member

parts.note: a limb is a member of the body

explanation.surface: The rise of a Conservative MP.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb is to go up or ascend.

clue.text: Incentive to suit slum elements

indicators.note: the words are broken into their elements, letters to be reassembled

explanation.surface: A grant to tidy up components of a slum.
explanation.definitionFit: A stimulus is something that spurs action, an incentive.

clue.text: Head back to view lost work

indicators.note: the work word goes missing from the view word

parts.note: an opinion is a view
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Turning the head back to look at a missing artwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head back' reads as an instruction, but it is the definition: the inion is the bump at the back of the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: The inion is the projecting point on the back of the skull, an anatomical landmark.

clue.text: If this is it you won't get it

definitions.text: If this is it you won't get it

parts.words: If this is it you won't get it
parts.note: something you cannot make sense of cannot be understood, so a clue of this description would defeat the solver

explanation.definitionFit: Something incomprehensible is impossible to understand, so nobody gets it.
